title: Week 97 · Lesson 121: Reproductive Life Planning, Contraception & Preconception Care — FNP-Level Shared Decision-Making & Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 97 — Lesson 121: Reproductive Life Planning, Contraception & Preconception Care

FNP-level goal: Provide noncoercive, person-centered reproductive care by connecting a patient’s goals, pregnancy potential, clinical risks, medication safety, access needs, and follow-up plan. Recognize when a routine contraception visit has become an urgent pregnancy, cardiovascular, thromboembolic, mental-health, or safety evaluation.

Learning Objectives

  • Open reproductive-life-planning conversations without assumptions about pregnancy desire, gender identity, anatomy, relationship status, sexual practices, or parenting goals.
  • Compare contraceptive categories by effectiveness, reversibility, user burden, bleeding effects, privacy, noncontraceptive benefits, contraindications, and patient preference.
  • Use the current U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria framework to identify methods that are acceptable, require careful risk-benefit assessment, or should not be used in a particular clinical situation.
  • Recognize high-yield safety issues involving estrogen-containing contraception, including hypertension, migraine with aura, smoking at age 35 or older, thromboembolic risk, postpartum timing, selected cardiac or liver conditions, and medication interactions.
  • Apply a structured preconception assessment that includes chronic disease, medication review, folic acid, immunization, infection risk, mental health, substance use, genetic or family history, and social safety.
  • Identify pregnancy and postpartum warning signs that require emergency evaluation or expedited obstetric, maternal-fetal medicine, or specialty collaboration.

Part 1 — Reproductive Care Is Longitudinal Primary Care

Reproductive-life planning is not a narrow birth-control visit. It intersects with hypertension, diabetes, epilepsy, migraine, depression, obesity, renal disease, anticoagulation, immunization, substance use, cancer risk, medication safety, sexual health, and social determinants of health. A patient may want to avoid pregnancy now, plan pregnancy later, be unsure, want to become pregnant soon, have no interest in pregnancy, or prefer not to discuss the issue. Each response deserves the same respect.

The FNP’s task is not to steer a patient toward a particular method or life choice. The task is to give accurate information, identify safety concerns, remove access barriers when possible, and support an informed decision. A patient may decline or discontinue contraception; reproductive autonomy includes that choice as well.

Part 2 — Begin With Privacy, Consent, and Patient Goals

Start in a private setting whenever possible. A neutral opening can be: What matters to you regarding pregnancy, parenting, or pregnancy prevention in the next year or longer term? Then ask whether the patient would like information, a method today, help preparing for pregnancy, or simply space to revisit the topic later.

Clarify confidentiality limits for adolescents and adults, local consent rules, and whether anyone is pressuring the patient about pregnancy or contraception. Reproductive coercion, intimate-partner violence, trafficking, financial dependence, lack of transportation, unstable housing, language barriers, and insurance restrictions can all change what is safe and realistic. Do not assume that a partner is safe to involve or that an electronic after-visit summary is private.

Part 3 — Build the Focused FNP History

A high-quality reproductive history includes current pregnancy possibility; last menstrual period and bleeding pattern when relevant; pregnancy, miscarriage, ectopic-pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum history; current and prior contraceptive experiences; method priorities; sexual practices; STI and HIV risk; cervical-screening status; and fertility goals. Ask about symptoms such as pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, dyspareunia, discharge, dysuria, fever, breast symptoms, headache, visual changes, chest pain, dyspnea, or unilateral leg swelling when clinically relevant.

Then connect the history to the rest of primary care: blood pressure, migraine subtype, smoking or nicotine use, thromboembolism, cardiovascular disease, liver disease, breast cancer history, diabetes, seizure disorder, renal disease, mood disorder, substance use, medication and supplement list, allergies, and current postpartum or lactation status. The question is not merely Which method is effective? It is Which option fits this patient’s goals and safety profile today?

Part 4 — The Contraception Method Map

Contraceptive care becomes easier when methods are organized by mechanism and user burden rather than memorized as an unconnected list. Long-acting reversible contraception includes intrauterine devices and the implant. Other hormonal options include injection, progestin-only pills, and combined hormonal pills, patch, or ring. Nonhormonal options include barrier methods, fertility-awareness approaches, permanent contraception, and the copper IUD. Emergency contraception addresses a recent risk event; it is not a substitute for discussing an ongoing plan if the patient wants one.

Effectiveness matters, but it is not the only outcome. Ask about desired duration, reversibility, menstrual effects, dysmenorrhea or heavy bleeding, acne or migraine history, comfort with a procedure, daily adherence, privacy, partner involvement, cost, timing of return to fertility, ability to obtain refills, and protection from STIs. Condoms and other barrier strategies remain important for STI risk reduction even when another method provides pregnancy prevention.

Part 5 — Shared Decision-Making Is the Clinical Skill

Do not present a method as the right answer because it is highly effective, convenient for the clinic, or common in a guideline. Instead, explain the tradeoffs in plain language and ask the patient to prioritize what matters most. For one patient, avoiding estrogen may be the decisive safety issue. For another, privacy, bleeding control, avoiding a pelvic procedure, immediate reversibility, or minimizing daily tasks may determine the choice.

Use teach-back for key information: how the method is used, what to do after a missed dose or device concern, expected bleeding changes, when backup protection may be needed, how to access follow-up, and which symptoms require urgent care. A method only works as planned when the patient can understand, obtain, and safely use it.

Part 6 — Use the U.S. MEC as a Decision Tool

The U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria is a clinical safety framework, not a replacement for judgment. In simplified terms, category 1 means no restriction for use; category 2 means advantages generally outweigh risks; category 3 means risks usually outweigh advantages and requires careful individualized assessment or an alternative; and category 4 means the method presents an unacceptable health risk in that situation. The category applies to a specific method and condition, so verify the current U.S. MEC rather than relying on memory alone.

This framework helps the FNP move from a vague concern to a defensible plan. For example, a patient with hypertension, migraine with aura, prior thrombosis, selected liver disease, or a relevant postpartum state may not be a candidate for estrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception. The next step is not to tell the patient that there are no options; it is to assess the condition accurately and discuss safer alternatives with the patient.

Part 7 — Estrogen Safety: High-Yield FNP Reasoning

Combined hormonal contraception can be clinically inappropriate in some settings because estrogen may add cardiovascular or thromboembolic risk. Measure blood pressure before initiating a combined hormonal method. Severe hypertension or vascular disease makes combined hormonal contraception unsafe; even controlled or less severe hypertension requires current MEC-guided assessment. Do not dismiss a markedly elevated reading as a contraception-only issue—confirm and evaluate hypertension according to clinical urgency.

Migraine history requires precision. Migraine with aura is not the same as migraine without aura, and a patient with new focal neurologic symptoms needs diagnostic evaluation rather than an automatic refill. Other high-yield considerations include smoking at age 35 or older, prior venous thromboembolism or thrombophilia, major cardiovascular disease, postpartum venous-thromboembolism risk, and medications that can reduce the effectiveness of some hormonal options. When the history is unclear, pause, clarify, and use current guidance rather than guessing.

Part 8 — Pregnancy Exclusion and Starting a Method Safely

A negative urine pregnancy test is useful but has timing limits. It cannot reliably exclude a very early pregnancy after recent unprotected intercourse. Use history and the current U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations to decide whether the clinician can be reasonably certain that the patient is not pregnant. Ask about timing of intercourse, current method use, menstrual pattern, postpartum status, breastfeeding, and recent pregnancy testing.

When pregnancy cannot be confidently excluded, some non-IUD methods may be started promptly with a planned pregnancy test in two to four weeks when clinically appropriate; IUD placement should wait until pregnancy can be reasonably excluded. This is a safety distinction, not a reason to create unnecessary access barriers. Document the reasoning, give clear follow-up instructions, and use the current CDC guidance and local protocol for method-specific details.

Part 9 — IUDs, STI Screening, and Infection Logic

An IUD visit should include pregnancy assessment, STI risk assessment, symptom review, and informed consent. If gonorrhea or chlamydia screening is indicated and the patient is asymptomatic, current U.S. guidance supports obtaining screening the same day without automatically delaying IUD placement when other criteria are met. However, do not place an IUD in a patient with current purulent cervicitis or known current gonorrhea or chlamydia infection; treat the infection and plan appropriate follow-up.

This distinction protects patients from two common errors: delaying effective care for a screening test that can be collected that day, and ignoring a known active infection. Pelvic pain, fever, abnormal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, or systemic illness should prompt evaluation for infection or another cause before treating the visit as routine contraception.

Part 10 — Emergency Contraception Is Time-Sensitive Care

Ask directly about recent unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, sexual assault, coercion, and timing. Emergency contraception should be offered promptly when pregnancy is not desired after a recent risk event. A copper IUD and emergency contraceptive pills are potential options; the most appropriate option depends on timing, current contraception, medical context, access, and patient preference. Ulipristal acetate has specific timing considerations before hormonal contraception is restarted, so verify the current U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations.

Emergency contraception does not terminate an established pregnancy. It is separate from abortion care, and it is not a reason to delay care for a person who later has a positive pregnancy test. Give a clear plan for pregnancy testing, ongoing contraception if desired, STI testing or prophylaxis when indicated, and trauma-informed support after assault or coercion.

Part 11 — Preconception Care Starts Before a Positive Test

Preconception care is preventive care for anyone who may become pregnant and for anyone actively planning pregnancy. The goal is not perfection before conception; it is earlier recognition and safer optimization. Review reproductive goals, prior pregnancy outcomes, age-related considerations, chronic conditions, medications, supplements, vaccines, nutrition, dental care, sleep, physical activity, tobacco or nicotine, alcohol and other substances, occupational exposures, environmental concerns, mental health, housing, food security, and support systems.

For average-risk persons planning or capable of pregnancy, current U.S. preventive guidance recommends daily folic acid 0.4 to 0.8 mg, or 400 to 800 micrograms, before conception and during early pregnancy to reduce neural-tube-defect risk. Higher-risk plans must be individualized; do not apply a higher dose to every patient without reviewing the indication and current guidance.

Part 12 — Medication Review Is a Safety Intervention

Review prescription medications, over-the-counter products, supplements, herbals, topical products, and medicines prescribed by other clinicians. Some drugs require a preconception transition plan because fetal risk, maternal risk, or both may change during pregnancy. Common examples that require careful coordination can include certain renin-angiotensin system medicines, antiseizure medicines, retinoids, anticoagulants, diabetes therapies, psychiatric medicines, and immunomodulators.

The safe teaching point is not stop every medication when pregnancy is possible. Abruptly stopping treatment can trigger seizures, hypertensive complications, psychiatric relapse, disease flare, return to substance use, or other harm. Instead: identify pregnancy potential, assess the indication and risk, coordinate with the prescribing clinician and obstetric or maternal-fetal medicine team as appropriate, and create a documented plan before conception whenever possible.

Part 13 — Chronic Disease Optimization Changes Pregnancy Risk

Diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, epilepsy, autoimmune disease, obesity, eating disorders, depression, bipolar disorder, and substance use can all affect pregnancy outcomes and medication choices. FNP care includes optimizing disease control, checking for complications, confirming a safe monitoring plan, and arranging the right collaboration—not promising that every condition can be managed alone in primary care.

For example, a patient with diabetes and hypertension who is planning pregnancy needs an individualized discussion of glycemic goals, blood-pressure strategy, kidney and retinal status, medication review, nutrition, and referral timing. A patient with epilepsy needs a coordinated plan that protects both seizure control and pregnancy safety. The clinical sequence is risk recognition, informed discussion, optimization, specialist collaboration when indicated, and reliable follow-up.

Part 14 — Immunization, Infection Prevention, and Genetics

Review immunization status before pregnancy whenever possible and use the current CDC adult and pregnancy schedules rather than a memorized list. Address STI and HIV screening based on risk, hepatitis status, travel or occupational exposure, and other prevention needs. Discuss family history, prior pregnancy complications, ancestry-associated conditions when relevant, and patient interest in genetic counseling or carrier screening. The FNP does not need to order every possible test; testing should answer a clinical question and be paired with informed consent and a plan for result interpretation.

Also address routine preventive care that can be missed when visits are framed only as contraception: blood pressure, diabetes and lipid risk when indicated, cancer screening, mental-health screening, dental care, and vaccinations. Reproductive care is an opportunity to strengthen the patient’s whole health plan.

Part 15 — Inclusive Care and Pregnancy Potential

Use anatomy- and behavior-based questions only when they are clinically relevant. Do not infer pregnancy potential from appearance, gender identity, relationship status, sexual orientation, or a patient’s stated wish not to be pregnant. Testosterone is not reliable contraception for a person with pregnancy potential. A respectful plan can address pregnancy prevention, fertility goals, medication safety, and gender-affirming care without making assumptions or forcing disclosure beyond what is needed for safe care.

Language matters. Terms such as patient, partner, pregnancy potential, and reproductive goals can preserve clarity while respecting identity. Ask the patient what words they prefer for their body and relationships, and document only the information needed for care.

Part 16 — Fertility Concerns and Referral Safety

Fertility evaluation should be tailored to age, menstrual pattern, duration of attempts, partner factors, prior reproductive history, and known medical conditions. Do not tell every patient to wait a fixed period if there are red flags such as absent or highly irregular menses, suspected ovulatory disorder, prior ectopic pregnancy, prior pelvic infection, known uterine or tubal disease, prior gonadotoxic treatment, or known male-factor concerns. Earlier evaluation or reproductive-endocrinology referral may be appropriate.

Fertility care should remain patient-centered. Some people need evaluation while planning pregnancy; others need contraception or counseling while they decide. These are not opposing clinical needs—both are forms of reproductive care.

Part 17 — Red Flags: When This Is No Longer Routine Outpatient Care

Emergency evaluation is needed for possible or confirmed pregnancy with severe unilateral pelvic or abdominal pain, shoulder pain, syncope or presyncope, hypotension, or heavy bleeding because ectopic pregnancy or another life-threatening condition must be considered. During pregnancy or up to one year postpartum, severe headache or visual change, chest pain, dyspnea, severe persistent abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fever, unilateral leg swelling or pain, seizure, severe vomiting with dehydration, or thoughts of self-harm require urgent assessment.

Expedited obstetric, maternal-fetal medicine, or specialty collaboration is appropriate for significant cardiac, renal, thromboembolic, neurologic, endocrine, psychiatric, or seizure disorders; poorly controlled chronic disease; complex medication exposure; prior severe pregnancy complication; or a condition in which pregnancy could pose substantial risk. Suspected reproductive coercion or intimate-partner violence requires a private, individualized safety response and connection to appropriate local resources.

Part 18 — FNP Case: The Estrogen-Safety Visit

A 32-year-old patient requests a combined oral contraceptive. Their blood pressure is 164/102, and they report recurrent headaches with visual aura before the headache begins. The FNP does not simply send a prescription because the patient is young. The FNP confirms the blood-pressure concern, clarifies the neurologic history, recognizes that estrogen-containing contraception may be unsafe, discusses non-estrogen options using current U.S. MEC guidance, and creates a plan for hypertension evaluation and follow-up. The key reasoning is risk assessment plus access to an acceptable alternative—not denial of reproductive care.

Part 19 — FNP Case: The Emergency-Contraception Visit

A 24-year-old patient presents three days after a condom broke. They do not want pregnancy, have no alarming symptoms, and would like a reliable ongoing method. The FNP addresses the time-sensitive event first: assess pregnancy possibility, offer appropriate emergency-contraception options promptly, screen for assault or coercion privately, and establish follow-up testing and ongoing contraception. A pregnancy test today may be useful, but it cannot erase the need to respond to recent exposure.

Part 20 — FNP Case: Preconception Medication Safety

A 30-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension, and depression wants to begin trying to conceive soon. They take multiple medications prescribed by different clinicians and ask whether to stop everything today. The FNP validates the goal but does not advise uncoordinated discontinuation. The plan includes medication reconciliation, pregnancy-safety review with the relevant prescribers, disease-control assessment, blood-pressure and glycemic optimization, folic-acid counseling, immunization and preventive review, mental-health support, and obstetric or maternal-fetal medicine collaboration when indicated.

FNP High-Yield Framework: PLAN

  1. P — Pregnancy goals and potential: Ask privately and without assumptions; assess timing, recent exposure, current method, and pregnancy possibility.
  2. L — Listen for priorities and barriers: Efficacy, bleeding, privacy, cost, procedures, adherence, identity, relationship safety, transportation, and follow-up all matter.
  3. A — Assess medical safety: Blood pressure, migraine aura, VTE risk, smoking, postpartum status, medications, chronic illness, STI symptoms, and mental-health or safety concerns.
  4. N — Navigate the plan: Use current U.S. MEC and Selected Practice Recommendations, provide the chosen method or urgent option when appropriate, give clear instructions, and arrange testing, follow-up, referral, or emergency escalation.

Take-Home Summary

FNP-level reproductive care is clinical reasoning, not method memorization. Start with autonomy and goals, then integrate pregnancy potential, safety, effectiveness, access, medication review, chronic-disease optimization, and follow-up. Verify method-specific decisions with current CDC guidance. A routine visit becomes urgent when pregnancy-related pain or bleeding, cardiopulmonary symptoms, neurologic symptoms, severe hypertension, infection, coercion, or mental-health danger is present.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized contraception, pregnancy, obstetric, emergency, or specialty care. Verify current U.S. MEC and Selected Practice Recommendations, local scope, formulary, and referral pathways before making patient-specific decisions. Call emergency services for severe symptoms or immediate danger.
